title: Incident review: AuthSSO outage
text:
Omar Brown: Okay, let's get started. This is the blameless review for the AuthSSO outage from yesterday, tracked as INC-2231. Agenda is timeline, root cause, why detection was slow, and then fixes with owners. I'd like to leave with named owners and dates for every action.
Omar Brown: Quick timeline from the incident channel. At 09:12 ET yesterday, login failures started spiking on AuthSSO. By 09:18 OMS was rejecting new sessions on the trading desk, and ClientHub and DocVault logins were failing too. We declared a Sev1 at 09:21. Service was restored at 09:58, so about 46 minutes of impact.
Angelica Schneider: I was the incident commander for the first twenty minutes. The first alert was actually from OMS, not AuthSSO. It was stale-quote warnings on the blotter side, so people jumped to MarketDataFeed.
Leo Martinez: Right, I was one of them. I spent about ten minutes in the MarketDataFeed ingestion dashboards. Everything was green there. Vendor lag was normal and PricingSvc was returning valuations fine. The staleness in OMS was just sessions expiring and not being able to refresh tokens.
Vincent Green: That's worth capturing. PricingSvc and MarketDataFeed never had a problem. The OMS alert text says 'quote stale' when the real failure is that the auth refresh is failing. That's misleading.
Omar Brown: Agreed, that goes in the detection section. Let's do root cause first. Vincent, you dug into the IdP side.
Vincent Green: Yes. The token signing key on the identity provider hit its rotation window at 09:10. The automated rotation job is supposed to publish the new public key to the JWKS endpoint before the old one stops signing. The job failed silently. A config change two weeks ago, ENG-4410, moved the secrets path, and the job lost permission to write the new key. So AuthSSO started issuing tokens with a key ID that downstream services couldn't verify.
Travis Dean: And that's why it hit OMS, ClientHub, and DocVault at the same time. They all cache the JWKS and only refetch on a miss. On a miss they got the old key set back, so verification failed.
Angelica Schneider: Also, the cache refetch has no backoff. OMS hammered the JWKS endpoint, so we had a retry storm on top of the real problem. That slowed the recovery.
Michael Jones: From the data side, I pulled the auth logs from DataLake. Failed verifications went from baseline to roughly 40 times normal inside six minutes. The logs did show the key ID mismatch clearly. We just had no alert on it.
Omar Brown: Good. So that's detection gap number one: no alert on JWKS verification failures. Gap two is that the rotation job failure didn't page anyone. Michael, can you build the verification failure rate query we can hand to alerting?
Michael Jones: Yes. I'll write it against the auth log tables and share the threshold proposal. I'd say alert at 5x baseline over a three-minute window. I can have it ready by Monday 2026-07-13.
Omar Brown: Great. I'll wire that into paging once you hand it over, target Wednesday 2026-07-15.
Leo Martinez: Can I raise the OMS alert wording? I can own changing the stale-quote alert so it checks session and auth health first and says so in the message. Otherwise the next person goes to MarketDataFeed again.
Omar Brown: Yes please. Leo owns the OMS alert text and a runbook link. Date?
Leo Martinez: Friday 2026-07-17.
Vincent Green: For the rotation job, I'll fix the secrets path permission today and add a dry-run check that fails loudly and pages if it can't publish the new key. I'd also like a pre-rotation check 24 hours ahead. Fix today, the pre-check by Friday 2026-07-17.
Travis Dean: What about the manual restore? It took us 37 minutes from declaration to fix because we had to find who had rights to publish the key by hand.
Angelica Schneider: That's a runbook issue. Only two people knew the procedure. I'll write the manual key publish runbook and run a walkthrough with the SRE rotation. I can do that by Tuesday 2026-07-14.
Omar Brown: Good. Then the client-side retry storm. Travis, you own the shared auth client library, right?
Travis Dean: Yes. I'll add exponential backoff with jitter on JWKS refetch and a short-lived grace window where the previous key set is honored. That needs a review since it touches security behavior. I'll open the PR by Friday 2026-07-17 and target rollout to OMS first in the next release after that.
Vincent Green: I'll review it, and I'd want Angelica on it too since she knows the OMS integration.
Angelica Schneider: Fine with me.
Omar Brown: One more item. Should we run a game day for key rotation in staging? I'd like to prove the fixes actually work before the next scheduled rotation.
Vincent Green: Yes. Let's force a rotation in staging after the pre-check lands. I'll schedule it for the week of 2026-07-20.
Omar Brown: Okay, let me read back the actions. Vincent: fix the secrets permission today, pre-rotation check by 07-17, staging rotation drill week of 07-20. Michael: verification failure query by 07-13. Omar: paging wiring by 07-15. Angelica: manual key publish runbook by 07-14. Leo: OMS alert wording and runbook link by 07-17. Travis: backoff and grace window PR by 07-17. I'll also write up the postmortem and circulate it by Friday. Anything missing?
Leo Martinez: Nothing from me.
Travis Dean: All good.
Omar Brown: Thanks, everyone. Closing the meeting.

title: Quarterly business review - Wealth
text:
Michael Castillo: Morning everyone, let's get started. This is the Q2 wealth QBR, Wednesday July 15. Agenda is four things: flows and AUM, portfolio performance and rebalancing, client service and onboarding, and then action items. Grace is out today so I'm chairing. Linda, want to kick off with flows?
Linda Barnes: Sure. Net new assets for the quarter came in at about $41 million, which is ahead of the $35 million target. Most of that was from existing households consolidating outside accounts, only about $9 million was truly new relationships. Attrition was light, two households left for estate-driven reasons, nothing related to service.
David Montes: On the new relationship side, the pipeline is decent, about eleven prospects in late stage. I'd say we convert six or seven by end of Q3 if the referral flow from M&A holds up.
Michael Castillo: Good. Tricia, performance and rebalancing.
Tricia Kelly: Model portfolios outperformed their blended benchmarks by roughly 40 basis points net for the quarter on the balanced strategy. The conservative sleeve was flat to slightly behind, about 8 bps under, because we were short duration while the front end rallied in May. I'd flag that as a known positioning call, not a process issue.
Michael Castillo: Agreed. Did the June rebalance run clean in PortfolioMgr?
Tricia Kelly: Mostly. We had a delay on the June 30 run because PricingSvc was serving stale marks on a handful of municipal bonds, and since PortfolioMgr depends on it, the drift calculations were off for about 90 minutes. We reran after Technology cleared it. No trades went out on bad numbers, but I want a check that blocks the run if prices are older than a set threshold.
Jonathan Chandler: Can I add, that same morning my advisors saw drift flags that didn't make sense, and we had no idea whether to trust them. A banner in the tool would help.
Michael Castillo: Fair. Decision: we'll ask Technology for a stale-price guard on rebalance runs. Tricia, you own that request, and please file it with Sam Okafor's team with the June 30 timeline attached.
Tricia Kelly: Will do, I'll file it today.
Michael Castillo: Next, client service. James, you had a couple of items on the low-risk households.
James Anderson: Yes. First, ⟨NAME_0234⟩ is one of mine, long-standing low-risk brokerage client, been with us since 2017. They asked to move to quarterly statements delivered electronically and to update their contact preferences. I've confirmed the request, but I want to re-verify identity before changing anything on ⟨ACCT_0480⟩. I'll call them on the number we have on file, which is ⟨PHONE_0232⟩, rather than responding to the email that came in.
Linda Barnes: Good call. Use the callback, not the inbound message. And log the verification in ClientHub.
James Anderson: Yes, already planned. I'll have it done by Friday.
Michael Castillo: Second item?
James Anderson: The review cycle. I have three annual reviews overdue from Q2 and I'd like to clear them before the end of July.
David Montes: I can take one of those off your plate if the household is already in my book. Send me the list.
James Anderson: Will do after the meeting.
Linda Barnes: On my side, ⟨NAME_0023⟩ has both a brokerage account, ⟨ACCT_0050⟩, and a cash management account, ⟨ACCT_0051⟩. They want to sweep idle cash from cash management into a short-term Treasury ladder. Risk profile is low so it fits, but I need Tricia to confirm the ladder construction.
Tricia Kelly: Happy to. I'd suggest staggering maturities over six months, so they keep liquidity. I'll send a one-page proposal to you by Monday.
Linda Barnes: Perfect. I'll send the summary to them at ⟨EMAIL_0023⟩ once you've signed off, and I'll set up a call to review.
Michael Castillo: Make sure the proposal goes through the normal suitability review before it goes out.
Linda Barnes: Of course.
Jonathan Chandler: One more topic from me, onboarding turnaround. Our average time from signed paperwork to funded account was nine business days this quarter, up from seven. The main drag was KYC clearance, waiting on document follow-ups.
David Montes: Right, and that's partly us. We send incomplete packets. I'd propose a pre-submission checklist for advisors so documents are complete the first time.
Jonathan Chandler: I can draft the checklist. I'll talk to the KYC team about what they reject most often.
Michael Castillo: Great, Jonathan owns that, draft by July 29. Let's aim to get back to seven days by end of Q3.
David Montes: Also worth noting KYCPipeline moves to Compliance ownership in October, so we should align the checklist with their intake requirements early.
Jonathan Chandler: Good point, I'll loop them in.
Michael Castillo: Let me recap action items. Tricia: file the stale-price guard request with Technology today, and send the Treasury ladder proposal to Linda by Monday. James: complete identity re-verification and the preference update for the brokerage client by Friday, and send David the overdue review list. David: take one of James's reviews and keep the pipeline conversions on track. Jonathan: draft the onboarding checklist by July 29 and consult Compliance. Linda: run the suitability review and client call on the cash sweep. Anything else?
Linda Barnes: Nothing from me.
Tricia Kelly: Nothing.
Michael Castillo: Thanks all. We'll reconvene for the Q3 review in October.

title: Executive staff meeting
text:
Catherine Hale: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for making it at nine. We have four things today: pipeline and desk updates, the KYC ownership transition, engineering resourcing ahead of Priya's departure, and the legacy reconciliation plan. Then we'll close on action items. Daniel, start us off with trading.
Daniel Reyes: Thanks, Catherine. July volumes are running about 12 percent above June in cash equities, and the desk is comfortable on capacity. The main thing I want to flag is OMS. It depends on AuthSSO, and we had two slow login episodes last week where traders were waiting up to a minute to get into the blotter. Nothing was lost, but during a fast market that is a real risk.
Sam Okafor: I can speak to that. Both episodes traced back to token refresh latency on the identity provider after a certificate rotation. We have a fix staged, and Omar's team will deploy it in the Tuesday maintenance window. We're also adding a synthetic login check so we're alerted before the desk notices.
Catherine Hale: Good. Daniel, are you comfortable with Tuesday, or should it go sooner?
Daniel Reyes: Tuesday is fine as long as it's after the close and not during the open. I'd like a rollback plan shared with the desk beforehand.
Sam Okafor: Agreed. I'll send the rollback steps to you by Monday.
Catherine Hale: Decision: the AuthSSO fix goes out Tuesday after the close, and Sam owns the rollback plan. Brian, lending.
Brian Kowalski: Pipeline is healthy. We're about $85 million in approved-not-closed commitments, and the closing team is working through a backlog from the end of the quarter. The one friction point is that LoanOrigination depends on KYCPipeline, and onboarding turnaround has been averaging four business days. That's slowing new relationships.
Ravi Patel: That ties into the ownership change. KYCPipeline moves from Operations to Compliance on October 6. My team has been running it, and I want to make sure we don't hand over a backlog. We've cut the queue from about 60 cases to about 25 over the last two weeks.
Catherine Hale: What's the plan for the handover itself?
Ravi Patel: I'd propose a written runbook, a two-week overlap where my analysts shadow Compliance, and a joint review of the open exceptions before the cutover. I'll draft the runbook and walk Marcus and Jenna through it.
Brian Kowalski: Can we get a target turnaround from Compliance after the move? If we can get to two business days, that helps us win mandates.
Catherine Hale: I'll raise that with Marcus, but let's not promise a number until the handover is complete. Ravi, runbook draft to me by August 14. Brian, send Ravi the lending exceptions that most often stall onboarding so they're covered in the runbook.
Brian Kowalski: Will do, I'll send those by end of next week.
Catherine Hale: Elena, M&A.
Elena Vasquez: We have three live mandates in diligence and two pitches scheduled for August. Fee pipeline is on track with the plan Martin shared last month, and we expect two signings before the end of the third quarter. The constraint is staffing. Two analysts are fully loaded, and I'd like approval to bring in a temporary contractor for modeling support through September.
Catherine Hale: I'm open to that. Send me the cost and scope, and I'll clear it with Martin. I'd rather not add permanent headcount until the fall pipeline firms up.
Elena Vasquez: Understood. I'll send a one-page request by Monday.
Catherine Hale: Thanks. Sam, engineering resourcing. Priya's last day is October 9.
Sam Okafor: Yes. Priya is the main person on the pricing and market data integration, so PricingSvc and MarketDataFeed are the areas I'm most concerned about. The plan is to pair Leo and Vincent with her on those starting next week, record architecture walkthroughs, and update the runbooks. I'd like that finished by the end of September so there is a buffer.
Daniel Reyes: Pricing is critical to us. If anything about PricingSvc is unclear after she leaves, the desk and Risk will feel it right away. Can we get a named backup owner?
Sam Okafor: Leo will be the named backup owner for PricingSvc, and Vincent for MarketDataFeed. I'll confirm that in writing to you and to Owen in Risk.
Catherine Hale: Good. Decision: Leo and Vincent are the designated successors, and the knowledge transfer is complete by September 30. Sam owns it. Last topic is ReconLegacy.
Ravi Patel: The legacy end-of-day reconciliation batch is still on Perl and Oracle 11g. It depends on SettlementEngine and GLCore, and last month we had two overnight runs that finished late and delayed break reviews. The long-term answer is to replace it, but that's a bigger project. In the near term I'd like Technology to review job scheduling and add monitoring.
Sam Okafor: We can do the scheduling review and monitoring this quarter. A replacement needs a proper business case and probably a vendor assessment. I can put together options and rough costs, but I can't staff it until the Priya transition is done.
Catherine Hale: Then we'll scope it now and decide on funding at the October staff meeting. Sam, monitoring and scheduling review by the end of August, and the replacement options paper by September 25. Ravi, give Sam the list of late-run dates and the downstream impact.
Ravi Patel: Will send it today.
Catherine Hale: Let me recap the action items. Sam: AuthSSO fix Tuesday, rollback plan to Daniel by Monday, successor documentation by September 30, recon monitoring by end of August, and the options paper by September 25. Ravi: KYC runbook draft by August 14 and the late-run data to Sam today. Brian: lending exceptions list to Ravi by next Friday. Elena: contractor request by Monday. Daniel: confirm the desk's sign-off on Tuesday's window. I'll speak with Marcus about KYC turnaround expectations. Anything else?
Daniel Reyes: Nothing from me.
Brian Kowalski: Nothing here.
Elena Vasquez: All set.
Catherine Hale: Great. Thanks, everyone. We'll reconvene next Thursday.

title: Vendor review: market data
text:
Angelica Schneider: Okay, let's get started. Thanks all for joining. Agenda today: one, the incumbent vendor renewal and the pricing they sent over. Two, latency and gap stats on MarketDataFeed for the last quarter. Three, the evaluation of the alternate vendor's consolidated feed. Four, credentials and access hygiene. Then action items. Barbara, can you start with the reliability numbers?
Barbara Beard: Sure. Over the last 90 days MarketDataFeed had three sequence-gap events from the incumbent's equities multicast, all under four minutes. One of them, June 17, bled into PricingSvc because stale quotes sat in the cache for about ninety seconds before the staleness guard tripped. Median end-to-end latency from the vendor handoff to our normalized topic is 3.2 milliseconds, p99 around 11. That's within the SLA in the contract.
Leo Martinez: Was the June 17 one on their side or ours? I remember the ticket, TECH-4417, but I never saw a root cause.
Barbara Beard: Their side. They did a failover between their two data centers without notifying us. Our feed handler resubscribed fine, but the recovery snapshot came in late. They gave us a post-incident write-up last week, and I attached it to the ticket.
Priya Raman: Which is a pattern. Their change notifications are the weak spot, not the raw performance. For the renewal I'd push for a contractual notification window, at least 48 hours for planned failovers, with credits if they miss it.
Angelica Schneider: Agreed. Kevin, you went through the renewal proposal. What are they asking?
Kevin Zhao: They want a three-year term with roughly a 7 percent uplift, taking us from about $1.34 million a year to about $1.43 million. They're also trying to bundle in the derivatives reference data module, which we don't use today. If we decline the bundle, the uplift drops to about 4 percent. The proposal PDF is in DocVault under the vendor contracts folder, and I've flagged the pricing schedule on page nine.
Vincent Green: Three years is too long if we're evaluating an alternate. I'd counter with a twelve-month renewal plus an option to extend, even if that costs us a point or two on price.
Travis Dean: Plus there's the redistribution clause. Last time I read it, display-only entitlements for the wealth team's PortfolioMgr screens were priced per user. That was a surprise during the last audit.
Kevin Zhao: Right, they counted about 140 non-professional users. Wealth has grown since, so the count probably needs a refresh before we sign anything.
Angelica Schneider: Good catch. Who can pull the current entitlement counts?
Travis Dean: I can. The user list comes from AuthSSO group membership, so I'll export the group list for the market data entitlements and reconcile it against what the vendor billed. I'll have it by next Wednesday.
Angelica Schneider: Great. Moving to the alternate vendor. Leo, you've been running the proof of concept.
Leo Martinez: Yes. We've had their consolidated feed in the lower environment for three weeks. Coverage is good for US and European equities, and the normalization is cleaner than what we do ourselves. But there are two issues. Their fixed income coverage is thin, especially for municipals and some corporate bonds, and their price for real-time options is about 30 percent higher.
Vincent Green: Thin fixed income matters for PricingSvc. If we lose evaluated prices for those bonds, the valuation fallbacks get ugly and RiskEngine's exposure numbers drift.
Leo Martinez: Exactly, which is why I'm not proposing a full replacement. The more realistic option is the alternate vendor as a secondary source for equities, which gives us a real failover when the incumbent has a gap like June 17.
Priya Raman: I like that, but the feed handler needs work to arbitrate between two sources. Right now it's single-primary with a manual switch. We'd need sequence-aware failover and a quorum check on price deviation, otherwise we might flip on a bad tick.
Kevin Zhao: I can scope that. A rough estimate would be six to eight weeks for one engineer including testing against replayed June data.
Priya Raman: Heads up on timing. I'm out after October 9th, so I want the design doc written and reviewed before then. I'll write the architecture section, and someone else should own the implementation.
Angelica Schneider: Understood. Kevin, you take implementation ownership and Priya is the design reviewer. Let's target a draft design by September 4.
Kevin Zhao: Works for me.
Barbara Beard: On the ops side, a dual-source setup means more alerting. I'd want a dashboard showing per-source latency, gap counts, and deviation between sources. I can build that off the existing metrics.
Angelica Schneider: Please do. Last agenda item, credentials. Travis, you raised this earlier.
Travis Dean: Yes. The vendor API keys and the SFTP credentials for the reference data drop are still shared in a team vault entry and haven't rotated in over a year. Longer term I'd like them moved behind service accounts that authenticate through AuthSSO, with rotation every 90 days.
Vincent Green: The vendor's API only supports static keys, though. We'd have to wrap it with a secrets broker rather than true SSO.
Travis Dean: Fine, a broker with automated rotation is still a big improvement. At minimum let's rotate now and remove the two people who've left the team from the access list.
Angelica Schneider: Agreed. Travis owns the rotation and the broker proposal. Let's do the immediate rotation next week during the Tuesday maintenance window so Barbara can watch the feed handlers.
Barbara Beard: Sounds good. I'll put it on the change calendar.
Angelica Schneider: Let me recap decisions. One, we counter the incumbent with a twelve-month term plus an extension option, decline the derivatives bundle, and request a 48-hour notification clause for failovers. Two, we pursue the alternate vendor as an equities secondary only, not a replacement. Three, we revisit fixed income coverage in Q4. Action items. Kevin: scope and implement dual-source failover, with the design draft by September 4. Priya: review and write the architecture section before she leaves. Travis: entitlement reconciliation by next Wednesday, credential rotation next Tuesday, and the broker proposal. Barbara: ticket the rotation window and build the dual-source dashboard. Leo: write up the proof of concept findings and put them in DocVault by Friday. And I'll take the counterproposal to procurement.
Leo Martinez: I'll have the write-up there tomorrow.
Vincent Green: Can I get the redlined contract sent to me before it goes to procurement? I want to check the redistribution language.
Angelica Schneider: Yes, I'll send it Monday. Thanks everyone, we're done.

title: Q3 town hall
text:
Linda Brandt: Good afternoon everyone, let's get started. Thanks for joining the Q3 town hall. Agenda today: one, department updates from Trading, Wealth, Lending, Risk and Operations. Two, the KYCPipeline ownership transfer. Three, the legacy reconciliation plan. Four, open questions and action items. Wendy is taking notes and will circulate them Monday.
Wendy Dyer: Confirmed. I'll post the notes and action list in #general by end of day Monday, and I'll put follow-up dates on the calendar.
Linda Brandt: Great. Daniel, let's start with Trading.
Daniel Reyes: Thanks, Linda. Volumes in the quarter have been solid, with the desk seeing higher flow in the last six weeks. The main thing I want to flag is OMS stability. We had two slow-login episodes tied to AuthSSO, and the desk lost a few minutes each time. Technology has a fix in testing. Second, we are adding two more quant strategies to the pre-trade checks, and Risk needs to sign off before we go live.
Owen Gallagher: Happy to do that, Daniel. We just need the parameter documentation at least a week ahead so we can run it through RiskEngine against the current limits.
Daniel Reyes: Understood. I'll have the documentation to you by Friday July 31.
Owen Gallagher: Perfect. Let me give the Risk update while I have the floor. Intraday VaR runs are completing on time, and the RiskEngine latency work we flagged last quarter is done. We've still seen occasional delays when PricingSvc is slow in the morning, since RiskEngine depends on it. We are tightening the alerting so we catch that before the desk does. We're also reviewing our concentration limits for the lending book, and I'd like to review that with Brian.
Brian Kowalski: Yes, please. On the Lending side, the pipeline is healthy. Origination volumes are up for the quarter, and turnaround on underwriting is down by roughly a day. The constraint right now is LoanOrigination, which depends on KYCPipeline. When KYC slows down, our closings slow down. So the ownership change matters a lot to us.
Linda Brandt: Good segue. Ravi, can you cover the KYCPipeline transfer?
Ravi Patel: Sure. As announced, KYCPipeline moves from Operations to Compliance on October 6. Until then Operations owns it, and we remain accountable for incidents. The plan is a runbook handover, an on-call rotation transition, and a joint review of the open backlog. We'll finish the runbook by end of August, then do two shadow weeks in September with the Compliance team. One risk: the pipeline depends on ClientHub, DocVault and SanctionsScreen, so the handover needs to cover those integrations as well.
Grace Lin: From the Wealth side, onboarding is the biggest pain point, so we're keen on this. Our advisors want a clear escalation path when a case gets stuck. Can we get a single contact during the transition?
Ravi Patel: Yes. I'll name an interim contact in Operations, and we'll agree on a Compliance contact before October 6. I'll send that out by August 7.
Grace Lin: Thank you. A quick update on Wealth. Assets under advisement are up on the quarter, mostly on market performance. PortfolioMgr rebalancing runs had a couple of delays when pricing data lagged. The team is also piloting a new client review template that cuts prep time. We'll decide on a full rollout at the end of August.
Linda Brandt: Thanks, Grace. Ravi, what about the reconciliation plan?
Ravi Patel: ReconLegacy is our end-of-day batch, written in Perl on Oracle 11g. It still depends on SettlementEngine and GLCore, and every break there lands on my team. The decision from the steering group is to start a replacement project in Q4, with parallel runs before we retire the legacy batch. Technology is scoping it. For now, the immediate action is to document the current break categories, so nothing is lost in migration. My team will have that written by August 21.
Owen Gallagher: Risk would like to be in the design review, since ReportingBI pulls from GLCore and we don't want surprises in the regulatory reports.
Ravi Patel: Agreed. I'll include you and your team in the scoping session.
Linda Brandt: Let me record the decisions. One, the KYCPipeline transfer date stays October 6. Two, the ReconLegacy replacement kicks off in Q4, with Risk in the design review. Three, the new quant checks need Risk sign-off before go-live. Any objections?
Daniel Reyes: None from Trading, as long as the sign-off doesn't slip past mid-August.
Owen Gallagher: We can turn it around within two weeks of receiving the documentation.
Linda Brandt: Good. Now questions. Anything from the floor?
Brian Kowalski: One more thing. Can we get a view of KYC turnaround times by week during the transition, so Lending can plan closings?
Ravi Patel: I can produce a weekly turnaround summary starting in August. I'll share it in #kyc-pipeline.
Linda Brandt: Perfect. Let me summarize the action items. Daniel sends the quant check documentation to Risk by July 31. Ravi names the interim contact by August 7, documents the recon break categories by August 21, and posts the weekly KYC turnaround summary starting in August. Owen tightens the PricingSvc delay alerting and schedules the Lending concentration review with Brian. Grace decides on the client review template rollout at the end of August. Wendy circulates the notes Monday. Thanks everyone, we'll close here.
Wendy Dyer: Notes will be out Monday. Thanks, all.

title: Risk committee monthly - 2026-07-30
text:
Paul Hansen: Morning everyone, let's get started. Thursday July 30, risk committee monthly. Attendees are John, Phillip, Angelica and me. Owen is out today so I'll chair. Agenda: one, July market risk and VaR backtesting. Two, credit exposure and watchlist. Three, RiskEngine and ReportingBI data issues. Four, actions and owners.
Angelica Li: Sounds good. I have the backtesting numbers ready whenever.
Paul Hansen: Start there then. Angelica, go ahead.
Angelica Li: So for July, 99 percent one-day VaR on the equity book averaged about 4.1 million, up from 3.6 million in June. We had one exception this month, on July 14, when the realized loss was around 5.3 million against a VaR of 3.9. That brings us to three exceptions over the trailing 250 days, which is still in the green zone but it's the upper end of it.
Paul Hansen: What drove the 14th?
Angelica Li: Mostly a gap in the rates-sensitive financials names after the CPI print. The desk was long a concentrated basket and the intraday VaR in RiskEngine didn't fully capture the correlation jump. The historical window we use is still weighted toward the calm stretch in the spring.
Paul Hansen: That's the issue I wanted to raise. I'd like us to test a shorter lookback with a stressed overlay. Can you run a parallel calc for August without changing the official numbers?
Angelica Li: Yes. I'll run a 125-day window plus a stressed period overlay in parallel and compare against the official VaR daily. I can have a first comparison by August 13.
Paul Hansen: Great. Action for Angelica, parallel VaR run, first comparison by August 13. Any objection to flagging it to the Head of Trading as an FYI?
John Garcia: No objection, but I'd keep it factual. The desk gets nervous when they hear the model is changing.
Paul Hansen: Agreed, I'll frame it as a diagnostic, not a methodology change. Moving on to credit. John, Phillip, you two own the watchlist.
John Garcia: Right. Total commercial lending exposure is roughly 412 million, and the watchlist is at 11 names, up from 9. Two additions this month. One is a mid-market manufacturing borrower where the debt service coverage ratio dropped to 1.08 times, under the 1.20 covenant. The other is a real estate borrower with a refinancing wall in the fourth quarter.
Phillip Jackson: On the manufacturer, I spoke with the relationship manager in Lending. The borrower has asked for a covenant waiver for two quarters. My recommendation is a conditional waiver, with monthly reporting of borrowing base and a fee, rather than an outright reset of the covenant.
Paul Hansen: What's the exposure?
Phillip Jackson: About 38 million drawn, 45 million committed. Internal rating is currently a 6, I'd propose moving it to a 7, which is special mention.
Paul Hansen: Any concern on collateral?
Phillip Jackson: Inventory and receivables, advance rates are 50 and 80 percent. Inventory turns have slowed, so I'd like the appraisal refreshed. That's the main open item.
John Garcia: I agree with the downgrade to a 7. On the real estate name, I'd keep it at a 5 for now but put it on the watchlist with a trigger. If the lender group hasn't signed a term sheet by the end of September, we move it to a 6.
Paul Hansen: Fine. Decision: manufacturer is downgraded to a 7 and a conditional waiver is supported by risk subject to the refreshed appraisal. Real estate name stays at a 5 with the September 30 trigger. Phillip, you take the appraisal follow-up and the waiver memo?
Phillip Jackson: Yes. I'll circulate the waiver memo by August 7 and have the appraisal request out to Lending by Monday.
Paul Hansen: Good. John, anything on concentration limits?
John Garcia: One thing. Our single-sector limit for industrials is 15 percent of the commercial book and we're at 14.2. title: Board risk committee - digital-asset clients
text:
Catherine Hale: Okay, let's start. Everyone has the memo I circulated last night. The proposal is a pause on onboarding new clients whose wealth derives from digital assets, effective tomorrow, August 22. Marcus, can you give the short version of COMP-112 first?
Marcus Bell: Sure. The OFS letter from July 28 says, in effect, show us you can evidence source of funds for crypto-derived wealth. Nadia's work on COMP-112 confirmed AMLMonitor can't trace on-chain flows. It sees fiat once it hits us through DataLake and FraudScore, but nothing before that. No blockchain analytics vendor, no on-chain data. So any attestation we take from a prospect, we can't test.
Catherine Hale: Owen, the custody side.
Owen Gallagher: Two points. Counterparty exposure to the custodians these clients use is concentrated in a handful of names, and our recourse if one fails is thin. And the exit question I raised in the channel: if final guidance comes out stricter than the interim, we'd be offboarding clients we just brought on. That's reputational damage and operational cost.
Catherine Hale: Grace, I want your view on the record.
Grace Lin: I'll be direct, I disagree with the pause. We have 14 prospects in the pipeline, about $40M of AUM, and nine of them are far along. Competitors are taking these clients now. An enhanced due diligence process with wallet attestations, exchange statements, tax records, would let us keep going while we find a vendor.
Marcus Bell: I understand that, Grace, and the documents help. But exchange statements show balances, not provenance. Without tracing we can't evidence where the coins came from, and that's the specific gap OFS called out.
Martin Osei: From the finance side, $40M of AUM is real but it's run-rate fee revenue in the low hundreds of thousands. One adverse exam finding costs us more than that in remediation and management time. I'm comfortable with a pause as long as it's clearly temporary and tied to conditions.
Linda Brandt: Operationally, what happens to the nine in flight?
Marcus Bell: We'd ask the RMs to hold them at the current step in KYCPipeline. Nothing gets declined, it just doesn't progress. We tell the prospect we're finalizing our framework.
Linda Brandt: Good. I'd want Technology scoping the AMLMonitor integration now rather than after a vendor is chosen. Sam's team can look at how on-chain data lands alongside the DataLake feeds.
Grace Lin: If we pause, I want the lifting conditions concrete. I don't want this drifting for a year.
Catherine Hale: Agreed. Two conditions in the memo. One, blockchain analytics integrated into AMLMonitor. Two, OFS publishes final guidance. Both, not either. Existing clients are unaffected.
Owen Gallagher: I'd add that on resumption we revisit custody limits, but that doesn't need to be a condition.
Catherine Hale: Fair, we'll take that as part of the resumption recommendation. Marcus, you own reporting back to this committee when both conditions are met.
Marcus Bell: Will do. I'll have Nadia run vendor evaluations in parallel so we're not starting from zero.
Catherine Hale: Let's vote. Pause on onboarding new digital-asset-derived clients effective August 22, lifting when both conditions are met, existing clients unaffected. Martin?
Martin Osei: Approve.
Linda Brandt: Approve.
Owen Gallagher: Approve.
Marcus Bell: Approve.
Grace Lin: I'll note my disagreement for the minutes, but I accept the decision and I'll communicate it to the team. Approve.
Catherine Hale: Thank you, Grace, that's appreciated. Motion carries. Grace briefs wealth advisors Monday, Linda will make sure Lending hears it from Brian. Thanks all.

title: IT Change Advisory Board - Thursday 2026-10-01
text:
Barbara Beard: Morning everyone, let's get started. It's 10:00, we have five attendees, so we have quorum for CAB. Barbara Beard: Agreed. First item, CHG-4471, DataLake cold storage tiering. Michael, that's yours.
Michael Jones: Right. The proposal is to move partitions older than 18 months from the hot tier to the cold object tier. Roughly 140 terabytes today, and it should cut our monthly storage spend by about $22,000. The migration job is throttled and runs overnight. Read paths stay the same, but queries against cold partitions will be slower, maybe 30 to 60 seconds on first read.
Omar Brown: What's depending on DataLake that would touch those old partitions? I'm thinking FraudScore and AMLMonitor, both critical, and CreditScoring.
Michael Jones: FraudScore and AMLMonitor mostly use rolling windows of 90 days, so they don't touch cold data. AML does have a lookback feature for the 24-month typology reports, though. That's the one that could hit cold partitions.
Omar Brown: That's the concern. If AMLMonitor's lookback job times out on a cold read, alerts could be delayed or silently dropped. I'd want that tested before we move anything.
Michael Jones: Fair. I can run the lookback job in staging against a cold-tier copy and report timings. I'd also suggest we raise the client timeout from 30 to 120 seconds for that job.
Kevin Zhao: Who owns that timeout config? I think it's in the AML ingestion repo, and I made the last change to it in August.
Michael Jones: Yes, that's the one. Kevin, could you prepare the config change as a separate pull request so it's reviewed independently?
Kevin Zhao: Sure. I'll have the PR up by Monday and tag Compliance Engineering for review since they own the monitor.
Barbara Beard: Okay. Risk assessment on this one: medium, because of the AML dependency. Rollback is straightforward, we can rehydrate partitions to hot tier, but rehydration of 140 terabytes would take around three days, so rollback isn't quick. Let me propose we phase it. Phase one is only partitions older than 36 months, which AML doesn't touch. Phase two after the staging test passes.
Michael Jones: That works. Phase one is about 60 terabytes.
Priya Raman: I support phasing. One more thing, make sure CreditScoring model retraining isn't scheduled in the migration window. I believe the quarterly retrain kicks off the weekend of the 10th.
Michael Jones: Good catch. Phase one would run the night of Tuesday the 6th, so it finishes well before that. I'll confirm with Lending.
Barbara Beard: Decision: CHG-4471 approved as phased. Phase one approved for the night of October 6th. Phase two is conditional on the staging lookback test results and Kevin's timeout PR merged, and it comes back to CAB for a go or no-go. Owner is Michael. Everyone good?
Omar Brown: Good with me.
Priya Raman: Approved.
Barbara Beard: Next, CHG-4476, the Oracle 11g quarterly security patch for ReconLegacy. Omar, you've been working on the plan.
Omar Brown: Yes. ReconLegacy is the Perl batch on Oracle 11g that does the end-of-day reconciliation. It depends on SettlementEngine and GLCore, so it can't run until both close for the day. Omar Brown: I remember. I tested in the clone environment on Tuesday and the batch completed, but only with the pinned driver version. So that's included in the plan.
Barbara Beard: What's the rollback?
Omar Brown: Snapshot of the database volume before patching, and restoring takes about 40 minutes. We'd have to decide by 03:00 to still be back before the 04:00 end of window.
Barbara Beard: Put that decision point in the change record. And I'd like a smoke test after: run the reconciliation for the prior business day in read-only mode and compare the break count against the saved baseline.

Barbara Beard: Decision: CHG-4476 approved for Saturday October 3rd, 02:00 to 04:00, conditional on written confirmation from Operations that no reruns are scheduled. Omar is the implementer, I'll be on call as backup. Priya, you'll review the rollback checklist.

title: ReconLegacy knowledge transfer #1
text:
Sam Okafor: Thanks for staying late, everyone. I know it's Friday at six. The goal today is the end-to-end batch flow, then the FX module and the month-end override. Tasha's here so we get the ops view of what breaks look like downstream. Priya, it's yours.
Priya Raman: Okay. Kevin, start with the crontab on the 11g host. Everything begins at 02:15 ET with one wrapper script, and it calls six steps in order. If any step exits non-zero, the wrapper stops and nothing gets posted to #recon.
Kevin Zhao: So the 06:30 post depends on every step succeeding?
Priya Raman: Yes. Step 1 pulls the SettlementEngine extract. Step 2 loads GLCore balances into staging tables. Step 3 does the match on trade id, account, and currency. Step 4 is FX adjustment. Step 5 classifies the breaks. Step 6 formats the report and posts it.
Kevin Zhao: Basic question: what happens if the settlement file is late? Does it wait?
Priya Raman: Step 1 polls for forty minutes, then aborts. That's the late-settlement failure in the runbook. You rerun from step 1 once the file lands.
Tasha Greene: From my side, that shows up as no report at 06:30. I usually ping #recon around seven if it's missing.
Priya Raman: Now step 4, which is the part nobody else has seen. It reads the FX rate table that comes from the PricingSvc snapshot. If the snapshot is older than the cutoff, the job aborts on purpose rather than computing breaks with stale rates. That's what happened after the PricingSvc incident in August, when I reran with --asof for 08-14.
Kevin Zhao: Why abort instead of using yesterday's rates?
Priya Raman: Because Tasha's team would get hundreds of false breaks and spend the morning chasing them. On July 22 the table loaded late and we got fourteen FX breaks. That was a partial load, which is worse than an abort.
Tasha Greene: Yeah, that morning was painful. All FX trades, all noise.
Priya Raman: Inside step 4 there's a tolerance hash keyed by currency pair. Majors have tight tolerances. A handful of restricted and thinly traded pairs get wider ones. There's also a branch that uses settlement-date rates instead of trade-date rates for same-day FX. That branch exists because GLCore books those on settlement date. If you change it, everything breaks.
Kevin Zhao: Is the tolerance hash in config or hardcoded?
Priya Raman: Hardcoded, unfortunately. In FxAdjust.pm, near the top. I'll comment every entry before I leave.
Sam Okafor: Can we capture which business owner approved each tolerance? We'll need that for the migration.
Priya Raman: Some of them, from old emails. I'll do my best.
Priya Raman: Last piece today is the month-end override. On the last business day, accrual entries hit GLCore after the settlement extract is cut, so the match would show false breaks. There's a flag file in the batch config directory. When it's present, step 3 excludes accrual account types and step 5 tags them for review instead of as breaks.
Kevin Zhao: Who creates the flag file?
Priya Raman: Me, manually, around six p.m. on month-end. And I remove it the next morning after Tasha confirms the accruals are in.
Tasha Greene: I didn't know that was manual. I just assumed month-end looked cleaner.
Kevin Zhao: What if someone forgets to remove it?
Priya Raman: Then real accrual breaks get hidden the next day. That's the risk. It should be automated, but it never was.
Sam Okafor: That goes on the ticket as its own item. Kevin, you'll do the October month-end flag yourself with Priya's notes, even though she's gone by then.
Kevin Zhao: Understood. Can I shadow a rerun before then?
Priya Raman: Yes. Monday I'll walk you through a --asof rerun on the test copy. We haven't touched the Oracle housekeeping scripts yet either.
Sam Okafor: Right. Realistically we need at least four more sessions before October 9: housekeeping and tablespace, a hands-on rerun, a full code read of FxAdjust.pm, and one for questions and the runbook update. I'll book them for next week. Kevin, clear your calendar as much as you can.
Kevin Zhao: Will do.
Sam Okafor: Thanks, all. Have a good weekend.
